title: NTA UGC NET English Full Mock Test #10
subtitle: 100 Questions · 200 Marks · Post-2018 NTA Pattern · Zero Answer Bias (25 A/B/C/D) · Reading Comprehension (Q91-100)

items.title: Mock #10 · Q1
items.stem:
Match List I with List II

List 1 [List

|Author |Work

A. John Keats |l. Alastor

B. William Wordsworth |ll. Songs of Experience|

IC. P. B. Shelley |lIl. Lamia

ID. William Blake IV. The Excursion

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Among the English Romantic poets, John Keats wrote the narrative poem Lamia (published 1820, A-III), and William Wordsworth published the long philosophical poem The Excursion in 1814 (B-IV). Percy Bysshe Shelley wrote Alastor, or The Spirit of Solitude (1816, C-I), and William Blake etched Songs of Experience in 1794 (D-II).

items.title: Mock #10 · Q2
items.stem: It was the first narrative on the life of a black woman slave to be published in England in 1831. It has profound influence on the abolition movement in Britain. Identify the book and its author
options: Mattie Jane Jackson – The Story of Mattie J. Jackson
Harriet Jacobs – Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl
Mary Prince – The History of Mary Prince
Elizabeth – Memoir of Old Elizabeth, a Coloured Woman
items.explanation: The History of Mary Prince (1831) was the first account by a Black woman published in Britain. Jacobs's book is American and from 1861.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q3
items.stem:
In the mechanical drill method of second language acquisition :
(a)
The learner has the freedom to choose from many responses.
(b)
The learner's response is totally controlled.
(c)
Comprehension of the item by the learner is not required.
(d)
Comprehension of the item by the learner is obligatory.
The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: As classified by Christina Bratt Paulston in second language pedagogy, a mechanical drill (unlike meaningful or communicative drills) involves complete control over the learner's response (b) with only one correct way of responding, and the learner can complete it without needing to understand the meaning of the item (c).

items.title: Mock #10 · Q4
items.stem: Stuart Hall belongs to __________ school of cultural studies.
items.explanation: Jamaican-born theorist Stuart Hall was a leading figure of the Birmingham School of Cultural Studies, serving as director of the Centre for Contemporary Cultural Studies (CCCS) at the University of Birmingham from 1968 to 1979.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q5
items.stem: Arrange the following works in the order in which they appear. Identify the correct code : I. No Longer at Ease II. Things Fall apart III. A Man of the People IV. Arrow of God The correct combination according to the code is : Code
items.explanation: Nigerian novelist Chinua Achebe's first four novels appeared in the following chronological order: Things Fall Apart (II, 1958), No Longer at Ease (I, 1960), Arrow of God (IV, 1964), and A Man of the People (III, 1966).

items.title: Mock #10 · Q6
items.stem: Who is the twentieth century poet, a winner of the Nobel Prize for literature who rejected the label "British" though he has always written in English rather than his regional language ?
items.explanation: Irish poet Seamus Heaney (1939–2013), winner of the 1995 Nobel Prize in Literature, famously protested his inclusion in The Penguin Book of Contemporary British Verse (1982) in his verse pamphlet An Open Letter (1983), declaring: 'Be advised / My passport's green. / No glass of ours was ever raised / To toast The Queen.'

items.title: Mock #10 · Q7
items.stem: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A): Culture is one of the two or three most complicated words in the English language. Reason (R): This is mainly because of several different though related meanings have emerged at particular moments throughout its long history. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
options: Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
items.explanation: In Keywords: A Vocabulary of Culture and Society (1976), Raymond Williams opens his discussion by noting that 'culture' is one of the two or three most complicated words in English because its meaning evolved historically from agricultural tending to intellectual cultivation and finally to an entire way of life, making Reason (R) the direct historical explanation for Assertion (A).

items.title: Mock #10 · Q8
items.stem: The New Historicists include
items.explanation: Stephen Greenblatt, Louis A. Montrose, and Jonathan Goldberg are three leading American practitioners of New Historicism in Renaissance literary studies, whereas Elaine Showalter is a feminist critic, Judith Butler is a queer theorist, and Raymond Williams founded Cultural Materialism.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q9
items.stem:
Women’s Studies is focused and built upon :
(A) Feminist critique of knowledge
(B) Cultural response of the native
(C) Political nature of the critical race theory
(D) The shift from liberal feminist views to more socialist and radical views of gender roles and culture
(E) Production of texts only
items.explanation: Women's Studies developed from a systematic feminist critique of traditional academic knowledge (A), accompanied by a theoretical shift from early liberal feminism toward socialist and radical perspectives on gender and power (D).

items.title: Mock #10 · Q10
items.meta: Unit VI: English in India: History, Evolution and Futures
items.stem:
Choose the correct statements amongst the following:
A. Macaulay was the practical man of affairs, helping and rejoicing in the progress of his beloved country.
B. Ruskin was like a Hebrew prophet just in from the desert, and the burden of his message was, “Woe to them that are at ease in Zion!”
C. Arnold was much like the cultivated Greek; his voice was soft, his speech suave, but he left the impression that you must be deficient in culture.
D. Newman was like the best French prose writers in expressing his thought with such naturalness and apparent ease that, without thinking of style, we received exactly the impression which he meant to convey.
items.explanation: Statements A, C, and D are authentic literary characterizations of Thomas Babington Macaulay, Matthew Arnold, and Cardinal John Henry Newman from William J. Long's *English Literature*. Statement B is incorrect because Long applied the comparison of a 'Hebrew prophet just in from the desert' shouting 'Woe to them that are at ease in Zion!' to Thomas Carlyle, not John Ruskin.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q11
items.stem:
Match List I with List II:

List I (Passages from Jonathan Swift)
(A) "When I found myself on my feet, I looked about me, and must confess I never beheld a more entertaining prospect. The country round appeared like a continued garden, and the inclosed fields, which were generally forty foot square, resembled so many beds of flowers."
(B) "There is likewise another great advantage in my scheme, that it will prevent those voluntary abortions, and that horrid practice of women murdering their bastard children, alas too frequent among us, sacrificing the poor innocent babes, I doubt, more to avoid the expense than the shame..."
(C) "Having to no purpose used all peaceable endeavors, the collected part of the semen, raised and inflamed, became adust, converted to choler, turned head upon the spinal duct, and ascended to the brain..."
(D) "Sweeping from butchers stalls, dung, guts, and blood, / Drowned puppies, stinking sprats, all drenched in mud, / Dead cats, and turnip tops, come tumbling down the flood."

List II (Titles)
(I) A Description of a City Shower
(II) A Voyage to Lilliput
(III) A Modest Proposal
(IV) A Tale of a Tub

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Passage A describes Gulliver viewing Lilliput (A Voyage to Lilliput, A-II); Passage B is from the economic satire A Modest Proposal (B-III); Passage C is the satirical account of religious zeal from Section IX of A Tale of a Tub (C-IV); and Passage D is the concluding triplet from the mock-heroic poem A Description of a City Shower (D-I).

items.title: Mock #10 · Q12
items.stem: Which of the following is an example of Functional Morpheme?
items.explanation: A functional morpheme is a free word that does a grammatical job, like 'and', 'the' or 'in'. 'Teach' is a lexical morpheme, while '-er' and '-ed' are bound morphemes.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q13
items.stem:
Which of the following are true in the context of Jonathan Swift?

A. He was born in Dublin and studied at Kilkenny Grammar School and Trinity College, Dublin
B. He co-authored a book with Samuel Johnson
C. He was ordained in the Church of Ireland in 1695
D. He was a member of Kit-Cat Club
E. He wrote the sensational novel Lady Audley's Secret

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Jonathan Swift was born in Dublin, attended Kilkenny School and Trinity College Dublin (A), and was ordained as an Anglican priest in the Church of Ireland in January 1695 (C). He was a key member of the Tory Scriblerus Club (not the Whig Kit-Cat Club), and Lady Audley's Secret was written by Mary Elizabeth Braddon.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q14
items.stem:
Listed below are the seemingly friendly characters in The Pilgrim’s Progress ho ive Christian
dangerous advice. Among them is one ho does not belong to this roup. Identify this odd
character.
items.explanation: In John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress (1678), Evangelist is Christian's trusted spiritual mentor who sets him on the narrow path to the Wicket Gate, whereas Mr. Worldly Wiseman, Ignorance, and Talkative provide perilous and false advice.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q15
items.stem:
Arrange the following statements in a chronological order:
A. Nissim Ezekiel founded Quest, a general intellectual review associated with liberal democratic politics.
B. The Illustrated Weekly of India sponsored a short story competition and began publishing contemporary Indian English poetry.
C. The Writers Workshop began to publish volumes of poetry.
D. C. R. Mandy became editor of the Illustrated Weekly of India.
items.explanation: These post-independence literary developments occurred chronologically as: C. R. Mandy became editor of *The Illustrated Weekly of India* (D, 1947), the magazine sponsored short story contests and featured contemporary poetry (B, early 1950s), Nissim Ezekiel founded the journal *Quest* (A, 1955), and P. Lal founded Writers Workshop in Calcutta (C, 1958).

items.title: Mock #10 · Q16
items.stem: Which of the following is not true of free verse ?
options: A dependence on the effective and more intense use of pauses
items.explanation: Free verse (vers libre) is open-form poetry that does not follow a regular metrical scheme or fixed rhyme pattern. Being 'written in iambic pentameter' describes blank verse or traditional metrical verse, not free verse.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q17
items.stem:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R
Assertion A: All modern languages have some words with pronunciations that seem to echo naturally occurring sounds.
Reason R: When different objects flew by, making a caw-caw or coo-coo sound, the early human tried to imitate the sounds and then used them to refer to those objects even when they weren't present.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: A is not correct but R is correct
Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is not correct
Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
items.explanation: In George Yule's The Study of Language, the 'bow-wow' hypothesis of the natural sound source explains that all modern languages contain onomatopoeic words echoing natural sounds because early humans imitated environmental sounds like 'caw-caw' or 'coo-coo' to refer to those objects.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q18
items.stem:
Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot
has
items.explanation: Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot (1953) is subtitled 'A tragicomedy in two acts' (corresponding to the fourth option where 'two' was omitted in printing). Its symmetrical two-act structure underscores the repetitive circularity of Vladimir and Estragon's waiting.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q19
items.stem:
K.S. Maniam is a major writer of Indian origin, writing in English, born and living in Malaysia.
Identify two of his novels from the following list.
(a)
The Rice Mother
(b)
The Return
(c)
Touching Earth
(d)
Between Lives
The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: Malaysian-Indian writer K. S. Maniam (1942–2020) is the author of the novels The Return (1981) (b) and Between Lives (2003) (d), whereas The Rice Mother (2002) is by Rani Manicka.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q20
items.stem: Nadine Gordimer is a :
items.explanation: Nadine Gordimer was a White South African novelist and essayist whose work vigorously challenged apartheid and racial injustice. She was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1991.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q21
items.stem:
Here is a list of Indian writers who have translated their work into English. Match the

items.title: Mock #10 · Q22
items.stem: The Medall, a poem written by John Dryden in 1681, is sub-titled
items.explanation: John Dryden's political poem The Medall (1682), written after the Whig leader Anthony Ashley Cooper, 1st Earl of Shaftesbury, was acquitted of high treason, bears the subtitle 'A Satire against Sedition'.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q23
items.meta: Unit IX: Literary Theory post World War II
items.stem:
The hermeneutics of suspicion is a term coined by Paul Ricoeur __________ .
(a)
to designate the postcolonial tendency to see theory and related reading anoeuvres
as a lobal conspiracy.
(b)
to describe interpretive bids that challenge and seek to overcome compartmentalized
cultural experiences.
(c)
ho, following Marx, Nietzsche, and Freud, held that textual appearances are deceptive
and texts do not racefully relinquish their eanings.
(d)
to describe a ode of interpretation that adopts a distrustful attitude towards texts in
order to elicit otherwise inaccessible eanings or implications.
The right combination according to the code is :
items.explanation: French philosopher Paul Ricoeur coined the 'hermeneutics of suspicion' in Freud and Philosophy (1965) to characterize the demythologizing interpretative modes of Marx, Nietzsche, and Freud, who held that surface meanings are deceptive screens (c) requiring a systematic hermeneutic of distrust (d).

items.title: Mock #10 · Q24
items.stem: The following postmodernist novel has an unusual protagonist whose gender is not revealed. So much so, that we keep wondering whether that person's relationships are homo-/hetero-sexual
items.explanation: Jeanette Winterson's postmodern novel Written on the Body (1992) is narrated in the first person by an unnamed, gender-unspecified protagonist who has a passionate affair with a married woman, Louise, deliberately subverting fixed categories of gender and hetero-/homosexuality.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q25
items.stem:
Chronologically arrange the following works in order of their publication.
A. Ariosto’s Orlando Furioso
B. Martin Luther’s 95 Theses at Wittenberg
C. The first Book of Common Prayer by Thomas Cranmer
D. Thomas More’s Utopia
E. Machiavelli’s The Prince
items.explanation: Niccolò Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513 (E), Thomas More published Utopia in 1516 (D), Martin Luther posted his 95 Theses in 1517 (B), Ludovico Ariosto published the complete 46-canto Orlando Furioso in 1532 (A), and Thomas Cranmer issued the first Book of Common Prayer in 1549 (C), establishing the order E-D-B-A-C.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q26
items.stem: "Imagined Communities" is a concept propounded by
items.explanation: Political scientist Benedict Anderson propounded the concept of 'imagined communities' in his influential 1983 book Imagined Communities: Reflections on the Origin and Spread of Nationalism, arguing that nations are socially constructed communities imagined by their members.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q27
items.stem:
Given below are two statements :— Assertion (A) and Reason (R) :
Assertion (A) : Many modern British writers infused their works with an extreme sense of uncertainty, disillusionment and despair.
Reason (R) : The Waste Land ends in a flurry of random allusions.
In the light of the above two statements choose the correct option :
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
items.explanation: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true: modern British writers expressed deep post-war uncertainty and disillusionment, and T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land (1922) concludes with a fragmented series of multilingual allusions. However, Eliot's ending is an illustration, not the cause, of modernist despair.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q28
items.stem:
In which play by Eugene Ionesco do you find the grotesque image of the leg of a corpse
thrusting onto the stage, and, which begins to grow larger as the play progresses in a menacing
manner ?
options: Amede or How to Get Rid of It
items.explanation: In Eugène Ionesco's absurdist play Amédée, or How to Get Rid of It (Amédée ou Comment s'en débarrasser, 1954), a middle-aged couple's apartment is progressively overtaken by a fifteen-year-old corpse suffering from 'geometric progression' whose giant legs burst through the bedroom door onto the stage.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q29
items.stem:
Which two of the following novels deal with the theme of apartheid?
(a) Purple Hibiscus
(b) July's People
(c) Cry, The Beloved Country
(d) The Mimic Men
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: Nadine Gordimer's July's People (b, 1981) and Alan Paton's Cry, the Beloved Country (c, 1948) are both landmark South African novels that directly confront racial segregation and apartheid. Purple Hibiscus is set in postcolonial Nigeria and The Mimic Men in the Caribbean.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q30
items.stem: In Keats's "Ode on a Grecian Urn" the key ideas are best described as the following except one. Which one ?
options: Scars of history versus consolations of art
items.explanation: John Keats's 'Ode on a Grecian Urn' (1819) meditates on the tension between dynamic movement and artistic stasis, fleeting human passion versus eternal painted love, and the famous equation of beauty and truth, rather than the 'scars of history.'

items.title: Mock #10 · Q31
items.stem:
Match List - I with List - II.
List - I | List - II
(A) The moment of protagonist's recognition in a narrative | (I) Catastrophe
(B) The decisive turn in tragedy by which the plot is resolved | (II) Chiasmus
(C) The inversion of an already established sequence | (III) Anagnorisis
(D) The figure by which something distasteful is described in less repugnant terms | (IV) Euphemism
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The literary terms match their definitions as follows: the protagonist's moment of recognition is Anagnorisis (A-III), the decisive tragic resolution is Catastrophe (B-I), the inversion of an established phrase sequence is Chiasmus (C-II), and describing something distasteful in milder terms is Euphemism (D-IV).

items.title: Mock #10 · Q32
items.stem:
Which novel by John Banville tells the story of a group of travellers who arrive on a small
island and stumble upon the house of Prof. Kreutznaer whose relationship to a painting
entitled The Golden World by a fictional Dutch artist named Vaublin plays a central role ?
items.explanation: Irish novelist John Banville's Ghosts (1993)—the second volume of his 'Frames' trilogy between The Book of Evidence and Athena—centres on a group of castaways on a small island who encounter Professor Kreutznaer and the mysterious masterpiece Le Monde d'or (The Golden World) by the fictional painter Jean Vaublin.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q33
items.stem:
Which of these constitute the preoccupations of the protagonist of Upamanyu Chatterjee's English, August?
A. Marijuana
B. Magic
C. Monotheism
D. Marcus Aurelius
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Upamanyu Chatterjee's novel English, August: An Indian Story (1988), young IAS probationer Agastya Sen copes with his alienation in the provincial town of Madna by smoking marijuana (A) and reading the Meditations of Roman Stoic emperor Marcus Aurelius (D).

items.title: Mock #10 · Q34
items.stem: Who among the following theorists formulated the concept of the utile dulci, profit combined with delight ?
items.explanation: In his verse epistle Ars Poetica (c. 19 BC), the Roman poet Horace formulated the influential critical maxim utile dulci ('profit combined with delight'), declaring that the ideal poet wins every vote by blending moral instruction with aesthetic pleasure.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q35
items.stem: The following is a list of key critical terms. Which is the right chronological order of their formulation?
options: The unconscious — langue — heresy of paraphrase — differance
Langue — the unconscious — differance — heresy of paraphrase
Differance — langue — heresy of paraphrase — the unconscious
Langue — differance — the unconscious — heresy of paraphrase
items.explanation: The correct chronological sequence of formulation is: Sigmund Freud's 'the unconscious' (c. 1895–1900, The Interpretation of Dreams), Ferdinand de Saussure's 'langue' (1906–1911 lectures; Course in General Linguistics, 1916), Cleanth Brooks's 'heresy of paraphrase' (The Well Wrought Urn, 1947), and Jacques Derrida's 'différance' (1963/1968).

items.title: Mock #10 · Q36
items.stem: One English poet addressing another : Thy soul was like a Star, and dwelt apart; Thou hast a voice whose sound was like the sea: Pure as the naked heavens, majestic, free, So didst thou travel on life's common way, In cheerful godliness… . Whose lines are these ? To whom are they addressed ?
items.explanation: These lines form the sestet of William Wordsworth's Petrarchan sonnet 'London, 1802' ('Milton! thou shouldst be living at this hour'), in which Wordsworth invokes John Milton's austere moral grandeur and republican virtue to rescue England from spiritual stagnation.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q37
items.meta: Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II
items.stem:
Given below are two statements, one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).

Assertion (A) : Spivak sees the project of colonialism as characterized by what Foucault had called 'epistemic violence', the imposition of a given set of beliefs over another.

Reason (R) : Spivak suggests that participation in the political process – access to citizenship, becoming a voter – will help to mobilize the subaltern on 'the long road to hegemony.'

In the context of the two statements, which one of the following is correct :
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
items.explanation: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak both analyzes colonial 'epistemic violence' (A) and discusses subaltern political mobilization toward hegemony (R), but the two statements address distinct aspects of her postcolonial theory rather than a direct cause-and-effect explanation.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q38
items.stem:
Which of the following statements are true about Modernism?
A. Modernism marked a break with formal conventions
B. Old ways of thought underwent cultural shift
C. Decline of liberal humanism
D. Modernism revived classical scholarship
E. Modernism promoted logocentric way of thoughts
items.explanation: Modernism was defined by a radical aesthetic departure from 19th-century realism and Victorian conventions (A), a profound cultural shift following industrialization and psychological insights (B), and widespread skepticism toward liberal humanist assumptions of inevitable progress after World War I (C). Statements D and E are incorrect because Modernism did not seek to restore classical scholarship nor advocate logocentric thought.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q39
items.stem:
Which of the following are correctly matched:
A. Jonathan Culler – Culture and Society
B. Raymond Williams – Literary Theory: A Very Short Introduction
C. Terry Eagleton – Criticism and Ideology
D. Walter Benjamin – Illuminations
E. Stanley Fish – The Implied Reader
Choose the correct option:
items.explanation: Terry Eagleton wrote Criticism and Ideology (1976, C) and Walter Benjamin wrote the essays collected in Illuminations (1968, D). Culture and Society is by Raymond Williams, Literary Theory: A Very Short Introduction is by Jonathan Culler, and The Implied Reader is by Wolfgang Iser.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q40
items.stem:
"The old order changeth yielding
place to new,

And God fulfils himself in many
way."

In which of the following poems do
these lines appear ?
items.explanation: In Alfred, Lord Tennyson's poem "Morte d'Arthur" (1842; later incorporated into "The Passing of Arthur" in Idylls of the King), the mortally wounded King Arthur speaks these famous lines from the barge to comfort his grieving knight Sir Bedivere.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q41
items.stem:
Match the title with the author :
(a)
Sexual Politics
(i)
Mary Ellman
(b)
A Literature of Their Own
(ii)
Elaine Showalter
(c)
Thinking About Women
(iii)

items.explanation: The feminist works match with their authors as follows: (a) Sexual Politics (1970) by Kate Millett (iv); (b) A Literature of Their Own (1977) by Elaine Showalter (ii); (c) Thinking About Women (1968) by Mary Ellmann (i); and (d) 'The Laugh of the Medusa' (1975) by Hélène Cixous (iii).

items.title: Mock #10 · Q42
items.stem: Penguin Books were prosecuted for obscenity and later acquitted for publishing a novel of D. H. Lawrence that makes a frank description of sex and an uncompromising use of four-letter words. Which of the following is the title of the novel?
items.explanation: In the landmark 1960 trial R v Penguin Books Ltd under the Obscene Publications Act 1959, Penguin Books was successfully defended and acquitted for publishing the full, unexpurgated edition of D. H. Lawrence's Lady Chatterley's Lover.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q43
items.stem:
Which among the following are appropriate about Latin American Literature?
A. There has been racial coherence and unity in literary representations of Latin America
B. The Latin American Literary tradition draws analogy between plant growth and human movement
C. Dzul Poot's stories depict the geography of the Chilam Balam Towns
D. Quechua had a wider popularity and presence across different nations.
E. The Latin American Literature is unitary and refrains from intertextuality of any kind
Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
items.explanation: As documented in Literary Cultures of Latin America, Mesoamerican indigenous literary traditions draw analogies between plant growth and human movement (B), Domingo Dzul Poot's Yucatec Maya tales depict the geography of the Chilam Balam towns (C), and Quechua enjoyed wide transnational presence across Andean nations (D), whereas Latin American literature is racially diverse and richly intertextual (making A and E false).

items.title: Mock #10 · Q44
items.stem: Who among the following was famous as a diarist?
items.explanation: John Evelyn (1620–1706) is, alongside Samuel Pepys, the most celebrated English diarist of the seventeenth century; his Diary spans several decades, documenting the English Civil War, the execution of Charles I, and the Great Fire of London.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q45
items.stem:
Arrange the following works of Criticism chronologically:
A. Gender Trouble: Feminism and the Subversion of Identity
B. A History of Gay Literature: The Male Tradition
C. History of Sexuality
D. New Lesbian Criticism: Literary and Cultural Readings
E. Bodies That Matter
items.explanation: The chronological order of these works in gender and queer theory is: Michel Foucault's *The History of Sexuality, Vol. 1* (C, 1976), Judith Butler's *Gender Trouble* (A, 1990), Sally Munt's *New Lesbian Criticism* (D, 1992), Judith Butler's *Bodies That Matter* (E, 1993), and Gregory Woods's *A History of Gay Literature* (B, 1998).

items.title: Mock #10 · Q46
items.stem:
In 1660, a group of 12 people including Robert Boyle and Christopher Wren formed what
they called the Royal Society.  In 1663, it became The Royal Society of London for Improving
Natural Knowledge.  What was the Society's motto ?
options: In the words of no one
items.explanation: Founded in 1660, the Royal Society of London adopted the Latin motto 'Nullius in verba' (adapted from Horace's Epistles), which translates literally as 'in the words of no one' (or 'take nobody's word for it'), affirming empirical experimentation over scholastic authority.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q47
items.stem:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: The poststructuralists' genre critics suggest that the way to 'de-essentialize' genre is to re-cast it in terms of discourse.
Statement II: But while the poststructuralist move toward dialectical exchange and ideology is both useful and necessary, conceiving of genre primarily in terms of discourse reveals certain limitations that are intrinsic to poststructuralism's basic approach to discourse and to the relationship envisioned between discourse and subjectivity.
In light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q91

Read the following poem and answer the question that follows:

Are You There?

My father and I shove back the furniture
to the four walls of the sitting room
then lie on the carpet wearing blindfolds,
his left hand holding my left hand.

Are you there, Moriarty? he enquires,
before tightening (I imagine) the grip
on his rolled-up copy of yesterday's Times.

There is only one possible answer to that.
I give it while rolling away to the side
but still clasping his hand, still in range,
and sure enough he manages a direct hit.

Now it is my turn, but the moment I lift
my weapon I realise there is no reason
to continue. I can tell from his stillness,
and the chill and stiffness of his fingers,
he has been dead for a good while already.
— Andrew Motion

options: to create space for more furniture.
items.explanation: In the opening lines of Andrew Motion's poem 'Are You There?', the speaker and his father shove back the furniture to the four walls of the sitting room to clear space on the carpet to play the blindfolded parlour game 'Are you there, Moriarty?'.

items.title: Mock #10 · Q96
items.meta: Unit IV / Unit VIII: Prose & Criticism
items.stem:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows:

In this sense, one can think of literature less as some inherent quality or set of qualities displayed by certain kinds of writing all the way from Beowulf to Virginia Woolf, than as a number of ways in which people relate themselves to writing. It would not be easy to isolate, from all that has been variously called 'literature', some constant set of inherent features. In fact, it would be as impossible as trying to identify the single distinguishing feature which all games have in common. There is no 'essence' of literature whatsoever. Any bit of writing may be read 'non-pragmatically', if that is what reading a text as literature means, just as any writing may be read 'poetically'. If I pore over the railway timetable not to discover a train connection but to stimulate in myself general reflections on the speed and complexity of modern existence, then I might be said to be reading it as literature. John M. Ellis has argued that the term 'literature' operates rather like the word 'weed': weeds are not particular kinds of plant, but just any kind of plant which for some reason or another a gardener does not want around. Perhaps 'literature' means something like the opposite: any kind of writing which for some reason or another somebody values highly. As the philosophers might say, 'literature' and 'weed' are functional rather than ontological terms: they tell us about what we do, not about the fixed being of things.

What is the implication of the statement: "In this sense, one can think of literature less as some inherent quality or set of qualities displayed by certain kinds of writing all the way from Beowulf to Virginia Woolf, than as a number of ways in which people relate themselves to writing"?
options: Literature has values that are constant and universal for all classes and races.
Literature has a moral dimension, which cannot be superseded by any other values.
The inherent quality of literature is its literariness.
Literature has values that may be interpreted differently by different subject-positions.
items.explanation: In this excerpt from Terry Eagleton's Literary Theory: An Introduction (1983), defining literature by how readers relate themselves to writing rather than by fixed, inherent qualities implies that literary value is functional and interpreted differently across different historical and social subject-positions.
